facts.fact_text: Some applicants complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully during peaceful demonstrations in support of LGBTI people.
On 17 May 2012 Mr Romanov took part in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 marked the International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia.
A group of people protesting against the 'Rainbow flash mob' event gathered nearby during the event on 17 May 2012.
The planned demonstration on 20 January 2013 in Voronezh was against the enactment of the law banning 'propaganda of non-traditional sexual relations'.
The authorities in Voronezh authorised the demonstration planned for 20 January 2013.

On 29 June 2013 Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova, Mr Fedorov and Mr Prokopenko took part in a demonstration involving about eighty participants in St Petersburg aimed at drawing attention to violations of the rights of LGBTI people in Russia.
The local authorities had been notified in advance of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg.
On 12 October 2013 Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina intended to take part in a demonstration in St Petersburg to mark Coming Out Day.
Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina arrived at the site of the demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg in advance and saw a group of counter-demonstrators.
On 3 November 2013 Mr Chechetkin attended the 'Rainbow Tea Social', a weekly event held to support LGBTI people, at an HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg.
Some applicants complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully during peaceful demonstrations in support of LGBTI people.
The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators started insulting the participants in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012.
About forty police officers were present at the site of the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh on 20 January 2013 but did not intervene.
All the participants in the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh on 20 January 2013 had to stop the demonstration and leave.
The police present at the scene of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg did not intervene when counter-demonstrators attacked the participants.
The police arrived about ten minutes after the beating of Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova and Mr Fedorov on 29 June 2013 and took the applicants to the police station.

The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators pushed Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina and prevented them from proceeding to the venue of the demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.
The attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013 was classified under Article 213 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as a disorderly act committed by a group.

On 23 October 2017 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin, stating that 'the attack had amounted to an administrative offence under Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation' ('battery').

On 19 March 2018 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin, essentially reiterating the reasons given in their first refusal of 23 October 2017.
No criminal investigation was ever instituted in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017.

The case concerns the respondent State's alleged failure to protect the applicants, all of whom are members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) community, from homophobic acts of violence by private individuals.
The case concerns the respondent State's alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation into incidents of homophobic acts of violence against the applicants.

The police present at the scene of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg did not intervene when counter-demonstrators attacked the participants.

Between July 2013 and December 2015 the police repeatedly refused to open a criminal investigation into battery committed for hate motives under Article 116 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation in relation to the attacks of 29 June 2013, citing a 'hostile attitude of people of heterosexual orientation towards members of the LGBTI community'.
All persons questioned by the police between November 2013 and February 2014 about the attack of 3 November 2013 alleged that the attack had been motivated by hatred against LGBTI people.
On 16 July 2014 the investigator suspended the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin on the grounds that the attackers could not be identified.
The investigators suspended and resumed the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin multiple times, most recently on 7 October 2017, without achieving any tangible results.

On 15 February 2018 a prosecutor quashed the police's decision of 23 October 2017 refusing to institute criminal proceedings and ordered the police to carry out additional inquiries, notably to obtain video-recordings from webcams, identify and question witnesses and obtain the opinion of a medical expert.
On 29 May 2018 a prosecutor quashed the police's decision of 19 March 2018 refusing to institute criminal proceedings and ordered additional inquiries.
On 28 December 2018 a prosecutor quashed the police's decision of 12 July 2018 refusing to institute criminal proceedings and ordered additional inquiries.
No criminal investigation was ever instituted in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017.
